title: Does Employment Protection Reduce Productivity? Evidence from US States
research_question: Does the introduction of dismissal protections that constrain employers' ability to terminate workers reduce employment fluctuations, alter firms' input choices (capital investment, capital-labor ratios, skill composition), and affect labor productivity and total factor productivity at the establishment level? Specifically, do increased firing costs lead firms to engage in capital deepening and experience declines in technical efficiency?
data_description: The analysis uses two confidential establishment-level datasets from the US Census Bureau covering 1976–1999. The Longitudinal Business Database (LBD), sourced from IRS tax records and Census surveys, provides annual employment and payroll data on approximately 3.9 million private establishments (about 68 million employees) across manufacturing, mining, construction, wholesale/retail trade, and services. From the LBD, the authors construct state-by-two-digit-SIC-by-year panels of employment levels, absolute year-over-year employment changes, and establishment entry/exit counts. The Annual Survey of Manufacturers (ASM) provides a balanced panel of approximately 5,700 manufacturing plants continuously surveyed from 1972 to 1999, with detailed operating data including total and production/non-production employment, quarterly production-worker employment, machinery and structures capital stocks (constructed via perpetual inventory using NBER and BEA deflators), capital investment, value of shipments, value-added, labor productivity, and total factor productivity. The unit of observation is the state-industry-year (LBD) or plant-year (ASM).
institutional_context: From the late 1970s through the early 1990s, US state courts progressively eroded the long-standing common-law doctrine of employment-at-will by adopting one or more of three exceptions: the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, the public policy exception, and the implied contract exception. These court-created doctrines exposed employers to wrongful-discharge litigation, increasing the uncertainty and potential cost of dismissing workers. Adoption timing varied across states and was driven by idiosyncratic precedent-setting cases brought before state high courts, with many states never adopting particular exceptions and a few reversing them. The good faith exception, adopted by only 13 states and most narrowly construed, is generally viewed as the most economically consequential. Personnel and legal trade publications amplified perceived risks, leading firms to anticipate substantial increases in adjustment costs. Prior research established that these doctrines raised hiring/firing costs and increased outsourcing to temporary help agencies, but their consequences for plant-level production choices and productivity remained unexamined.
ground_truth_notes: The results are tentative due to potential confounding economic shocks and implausibly large subsequent growth in manufacturing employment.
